title: How to create a variable in Figma on Mac: step by step for beginners
metaTitle: How to create a variable in Figma on Mac (step by step)
description: Find out how to create a variable in Figma on Mac: open the Variables tab, pick a collection, then name and set the value. Steps for the desktop app.
targetKeyword: how to create a variable in figma on mac
intro: To create a variable in Figma on Mac, open a file you can edit, click the Variables tab in the left navigation bar, and open a collection. Then click + Create variable, choose a type from the dropdown, and enter a name and a value.
tldr: Open a file you can edit, then click the Variables tab in the left navigation bar.
Open a collection, click + Create variable, and pick a type from the dropdown.
Type a name in the first column and a value in the second column.
Create a new collection from More options > Create collection in the variables sidebar.

blocks.text: Variables are named values you reuse across a file. A brand color, a spacing value or a font size can live in one place. When you change the value, every layer that uses it follows.
Check access, plan and version before you start
Variables need edit access to the file. If someone gave you view access, ask the file owner to change it before you start. Otherwise the steps below will stop at the first click.
Variables are listed as available on all plans. Publishing variables to team libraries and using them in prototypes need a Professional, Education, Organization, Government or Enterprise plan.

items: Confirm you have edit access to the file you want to change.
Open the Figma desktop app for Mac, the version this guide covers.
Check your plan if you need team libraries, prototypes or extra modes.
Update the app if the Variables tab is missing. The update steps are later in this guide.

blocks.text: Find the Variables tab in the left navigation bar

Figma moved the entry point for variables. Older guides tell you to deselect everything on the canvas, then look in the Properties panel for a Local variables tab. Figma's help center now says to click the Variables tab in the left navigation bar.

A Figma moderator wrote on January 28, 2026 that the change was rolling out as an updated navigation bar. Your file may still show the older layout, so the screen can look a little different. The moderator named 126.0.4 as the latest desktop version at that time.
If you cannot find the tab, update the app before you change anything else. Do not hunt through menus for a hidden option. The update check takes a minute.
Create a variable with a worked example

Here is a worked example. Say you want one brand blue for buttons, links and headers. You create a color variable called brand blue, then use it on each element instead of picking the color by hand every time.

Open a collection before you add anything. Many people keep one collection for colors and another for spacing or type. Choose the type in the dropdown first, since the type decides what kind of value you can enter.
Naming matters more than people expect. Name each variable for its purpose, not its current value. A name that says what it is for keeps working even when the color changes.

items: Good names: brand blue, text muted, card padding, button label
Weak names: blue final, new blue, blue copy again, misc color
Test: would a teammate know what the variable is for from its name alone?

blocks.text: Enter names and values in the right columns
The first column holds the variable name. The second column holds the value. If your plan allows extra modes, more columns appear, and each one stores another value for the same variable.

Match the value to the type. A color variable needs a color value. A number variable needs a number, and a string variable needs text. Mismatched values are the quickest way to confuse yourself later.
Move on once the row looks right. You can change names and values later, so do not stall on the first one. Build a small set first, then refine it after you use it in a real layer.
Edit a variable name, description and code names
Hover over the variable's row and click the Edit variable icon. The modal lets you change the name and description, edit the values and set the code syntax.

Code syntax gives the variable one name per platform: Web, Android and iOS. A variable can have up to three of these names. Use them when developers read the same token in code and need a platform-specific name.
The Hide from publishing option keeps a variable out of what you publish. Use it for helpers or drafts that your team should not pick up by accident.
Limit where a variable shows with scopes
Scopes control where a variable appears when you pick values. Scoping is available for number, color and string variables. Open the Scope tab inside the Edit variable modal to set it.
The Show in all checkbox is the simplest setting. Clear it when you want the variable only in certain fields. A corner radius number does not belong in the fill color picker, for example.
Scopes are easy to forget. When a value is missing from a picker, check the scope before you assume the variable is broken.
Select, duplicate and rename variables quickly
Hold Command (⌘) and click each variable you want to select. Hold Shift and click to select a range, from the first variable to the last.

After you select, press Shift + Enter to duplicate. Duplicating beats starting from scratch when two variables differ by only one value. Rename the copy right away, or you will end up with two rows that look the same.
Create a new collection and add variables to it
Collections group related variables. To make one, open the variables modal, click More options in the sidebar, then choose Create collection.
Figma's help page says you need a variable before you create a new collection. Add one to a collection you already have, then create the new one.
A small color collection makes a good first project. Add a main color, a muted text color and a background color. Then apply each one to real layers to check that the values behave as you expect.

blocks.caption: Limits as stated on Figma's help center pages, checked November 7, 2026

blocks.text: Figma's help page does not give a per-collection mode limit. It does say each collection can hold up to 5,000 variables. Those are the numbers you can rely on from the help center.
Check your plan in your Figma account before you design a file around modes. The table is a starting point, not a substitute for your account page.
Fix common problems with variables
Several problems come up in Figma's community forum. Each one has a different cause, and none of the threads has an official fix.

items: Variables tab missing: update the app, then check whether the file still shows the older layout.
Mode switching greyed out: community members point to one variable not on the latest version, hidden layers or out-of-sync libraries.
Duplicate collections greyed out: a forum member suggested enabling All collections under Collection options, or disabling other libraries. The thread does not confirm a fix.

blocks.text: If your problem is not on this list, post your Figma version, your plan and the exact message in the community forum. Specific details get better answers than a vague complaint.

blocks.title: Check before you delete
blocks.text: Greyed out collections can come from libraries or other files. Do not delete one until you know where it came from.
Update Figma on Mac and check the version
Click Figma in the menu bar, then choose Figma > Check for Updates. If you do not see an update option, your Mac may be managed by IT.

Figma says that on admin-managed Macs where the app folder is not writable, it supports desktop app versions only for up to two months. Auto-updates for installs in the Applications folder need write access to the Figma app bundle.
Keyboard shortcuts for variables on a Mac

Figma's keyboard guide does not list a Mac shortcut for opening the Variables panel. It also leaves out shortcuts for Layers, Assets and Properties. The shortcuts below cover the variable work itself, plus the panel that lists every shortcut.

Some third-party guides claim a shortcut for variables. Figma's own pages do not list one, so test any shortcut on your own Mac before you rely on it. A 2023 forum reply pointed to the Toggle variables option in the quick actions toolbar, opened from the Figma logo at the top left.
Mistakes people make with variables

items: Naming variables after their value, like blue final, so the name stops making sense.
Forgetting the scope, then assuming the variable is broken.
Creating a new collection before adding any variable, then getting stuck.
Duplicating a variable and forgetting to rename the copy.
Trusting a shortcut from a guide without testing it first.

blocks.text: Most of these mistakes come down to naming and scope. Fix those first, and the rest of the file stays easier to read.
What to do after your first variable works
Apply the variable to a few real layers first. Change its value and check that the layers update. This is the fastest test that the setup works.

Then build out the rest of your system. Text styles, components and frames are common next steps. These guides cover them in order: [create a text style](/how-to/create-a-text-style-in-figma), [create a component](/how-to/create-a-component-in-figma) and [create a frame](/how-to/create-a-frame-in-figma).
Keep your first collection small. Add more once you trust the names and the scopes. A small system is easier to fix when something goes wrong.

faq.question: Where is the Variables tab in Figma on Mac?
faq.answer: In current Figma desktop versions, click the Variables tab in the left navigation bar. Older files may still show a Local variables tab in the Properties panel when nothing is selected on the canvas. Figma's help center describes the left navigation bar as the new entry point.

faq.question: Is there a keyboard shortcut to open variables on Mac?
faq.answer: Figma's keyboard guide does not list one. Some third-party guides claim a shortcut, and a 2023 forum reply pointed to the quick actions toolbar. Test any shortcut on your own Mac before you rely on it.

faq.question: Can I create variables on every Figma plan?
faq.answer: Figma lists variables as available on all plans, and creating them needs edit access to the file. Publishing to team libraries and using variables in prototypes need a Professional, Education, Organization, Government or Enterprise plan.

faq.question: How many variables can one collection hold?
faq.answer: Each collection can hold up to 5,000 variables, according to Figma's help center. The limit applies per collection, so a large system can use more than one collection.

faq.question: Why can't I add a second value column?
faq.answer: Extra columns, which Figma calls modes, need an Education or paid plan. If your plan does not include them, check your plan before you look for a bug in the file.

faq.question: Why is my variable mode switch greyed out?
faq.answer: Community members report that one variable not on the latest version, hidden layers or out-of-sync libraries can block mode switching. The thread has no official fix, so check each of those first.

faq.question: Do I need to update Figma to see the Variables tab?
faq.answer: You might. Figma said in January 2026 that the new navigation bar was rolling out as an update, and a moderator named 126.0.4 as the latest desktop version then. Open Figma > Check for Updates to see what your Mac runs.

steps.name: Open a file you can edit
steps.text: Open the Figma desktop app on your Mac and open the file. Variables need edit access to the file, so open one where you can make changes.
steps.tip: If the file is shared with you as view only, ask the owner for edit access first.

steps.name: Click the Variables tab
steps.text: In the left navigation bar, click the Variables tab. This opens the variables modal, with your collections listed in a sidebar.
steps.tip: If you do not see the tab, check for updates before you look elsewhere.

steps.name: Open a collection
steps.text: Click a collection in the sidebar of the variables modal. Each collection holds its own variables. If you have none yet, create one using the steps near the end of this guide.

steps.name: Click + Create variable
steps.text: Click + Create variable inside the open collection. Figma adds a new variable to that collection, ready for a name.

steps.name: Choose a type
steps.text: Open the type dropdown and pick the variable type. Color, number and string are the types Figma's scope settings cover, so start with one of those.
steps.tip: Pick color for a brand blue, and number for a spacing value.

steps.name: Enter the name
steps.text: Type a name in the first column. Use a name that says what the value is for, such as brand blue or card padding.
steps.tip: Avoid names that describe only the value, because they break when the value changes.

steps.name: Enter the value
steps.text: Type the value in the second column. The value must match the type you picked, so a color variable needs a color value.

steps.name: Duplicate similar variables
steps.text: Command-click each variable you want to copy, then press Shift + Enter. Rename each copy right away.
steps.tip: A copy with the old name is the most common source of duplicate rows.

steps.name: Edit a variable's details
steps.text: Hover over the variable's row and click the Edit variable icon. The Edit variable modal opens with the name, description, values and code syntax.

steps.name: Set the scope
steps.text: In the Edit variable modal, open the Scope tab. Clear Show in all if you want to limit where the variable appears. Scopes work for number, color and string variables.
steps.tip: If a value is missing from a picker, check this tab first.

steps.name: Create a new collection
steps.text: In the sidebar of the variables modal, click More options, then Create collection. Figma's help page says you need a variable first, so add one to an existing collection before you start.

steps.name: Check for updates if the tab is missing
steps.text: Click Figma in the menu bar, then choose Check for Updates. Reopen your file and look for the Variables tab again.
steps.tip: On an IT-managed Mac, ask IT for the update instead of forcing it.

troubleshooting.fix: Update Figma with Figma > Check for Updates. Older files may still show a Local variables tab in the Properties panel when nothing is selected on the canvas.
Community members say one variable not on the latest version, hidden layers or out-of-sync libraries can block it. Fix those first. The thread has no official fix.

troubleshooting.problem: Duplicate collections are greyed out and cannot be deleted
troubleshooting.fix: A forum member suggested enabling All collections under Collection options, or disabling other libraries. That thread does not confirm a fix, so test on a copy of the file first.

troubleshooting.problem: I cannot add a second value column
troubleshooting.fix: Extra modes need an Education or paid plan, according to Figma's help center. Check your plan before you troubleshoot further.

troubleshooting.problem: My Mac's Figma version is stuck
troubleshooting.fix: On admin-managed Macs where the app folder is not writable, Figma supports desktop versions for up to two months. Ask IT to update the app.

troubleshooting.problem: I cannot find a shortcut for variables
troubleshooting.fix: Figma's keyboard guide does not list one. Press Control, Shift and question mark to see the current shortcuts list, and ask in the Figma forum if a shortcut is missing.
